clue.text: Genial chap needing no introduction on Malta

indicators.note: an introduction is the opening, so the word for chap loses its first letter

parts.note: M is the international vehicle code for Malta
a chap is a fellow

explanation.surface: A friendly man who is so well known on Malta that nobody needs to introduce him.
explanation.walkthrough: 'On' in an across clue places the following piece after the island's letter. M is Malta's international vehicle code.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone mellow is relaxed, warm and good-humoured, which is what a genial person is.

clue.text: Involved with blocking river up when demented

indicators.note: in a down entry, going up means reading the river's name from bottom to top
something blocking a channel sits inside it, so one piece lodges within the other

parts.note: the Cam is the river through Cambridge
to be in on something is to be involved

explanation.surface: Someone caught up in damming a river goes out of their mind.
explanation.walkthrough: MAC (the Cam upside down) is split by IN, giving MANIC.
explanation.definitionFit: Manic and demented both describe wild, frenzied behaviour, as if out of one's mind; they are synonyms here.

clue.text: Capone turned up with clothing in a case

indicators.note: turned up in a down entry means the gangster's short name is read from the bottom

parts.note: AL Capone, the gangster, read upwards
W is the standard abbreviation for with
a suit is a set of clothing

explanation.surface: Al Capone appeared carrying clothes in a suitcase.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Case' looks like luggage holding the clothing, but it is the definition: a court case.
explanation.definitionFit: A lawsuit is a legal action brought in court, which is what a case means in law.

clue.text: I slap it on furiously with what Rembrandt liked to use

indicators.note: slapping paint about furiously throws the letters into a wild new order

parts.note: the letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: An artist daubing canvas wildly with the medium of the old Dutch masters.
explanation.definitionFit: Rembrandt worked chiefly in oils, so oil paints are the medium he favoured.

clue.text: Foolish sailors game to return to Germany

parts.note: ABs are able seamen

indicators.note: something returning comes back the way it went, so the game's letters run backwards

parts.note: RU is rugby union
D is the vehicle code for Germany (Deutschland)

explanation.surface: Silly sailors whose match is heading back to Germany.
explanation.definitionFit: Absurd means ridiculous or senseless, the same as foolish.

clue.text: Crack reportedly found in stopper

indicators.note: reportedly means as heard said, so we want a word that is said like the one for crack

parts.note: a crack is a break

explanation.surface: A crack has been discovered in a bottle stopper.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stopper' suggests a cork; here it is something that stops a vehicle.
explanation.definitionFit: A brake is the device that halts a wheel or vehicle, literally a stopper.

clue.text: Just winning over the Conservatives

parts.note: a team that is up is winning
the Conservatives are the political right

explanation.surface: A political party that has only narrowly beaten the Tories.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Over' places one piece above the other in this down entry. 'Just' looks like 'barely' but is an adjective meaning fair.
explanation.definitionFit: An upright person is honest and principled, which is what just means of a person.

clue.text: Follow with arrest when it's found on a clergyman

definitions.note: a descriptive phrase standing for the thing itself

parts.note: to dog someone is to follow them
police slang: to collar is to arrest

explanation.surface: A clergyman is tailed and arrested.
explanation.walkthrough: 'With' simply joins the two verbs.
explanation.definitionFit: A dog collar is the white band worn round a cleric's neck, so it is what you see on a clergyman.

clue.text: Wise guy's denial heard by everyone

indicators.note: heard means we take the sound of the denial rather than its spelling

parts.note: a denial is a no
everyone is all

explanation.surface: A smart alec says no and everybody hears it.
explanation.definitionFit: A know-all is someone who acts as if they know everything, a sarcastic wise guy or smart alec.

clue.text: Bombardment of boat carrying soldiers

indicators.note: a vessel carrying something holds it inside, so one word goes within the other

parts.note: a barge is a flat-bottomed boat
RA is the Royal Artillery

explanation.surface: A troopship coming under heavy fire.
explanation.definitionFit: A barrage is a concentrated artillery attack, a sustained bombardment.

clue.text: One ready to serve for a short time on island

parts.note: a minute is a short time
the Isle of Man

explanation.surface: A volunteer prepared to do a brief stint of service on an island.
explanation.walkthrough: 'On' puts one piece above the other in this down entry. The Isle of Man lies between Britain and Ireland.
explanation.definitionFit: Minutemen were American colonial militia pledged to turn out for battle at a moment's notice.

clue.text: It's a case of working without us in Central America

indicators.note: without in its old sense of outside, so the working word goes round everything else

parts.note: active means working

indicators.note: the pronoun sits inside the region's two-letter abbreviation

parts.note: the usual abbreviation for Central America
taken as written

explanation.surface: Something like a legal case concerning people working abroad without Americans.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Without' is used in its old sense of outside, and there are two nested insertions. 'Case' here is grammar, not law.
explanation.definitionFit: The accusative is the grammatical case marking a verb's direct object in languages such as Latin and German.

clue.text: Prison officer's first to stab convict from behind

indicators.note: coming from behind means the convict's word is read back to front
stabbing pushes something into a body, so one piece goes inside the other

parts.note: an old lag is a long-serving convict

indicators.note: first asks for only the opening letter of the official's word

parts.note: the opening letter of the word

explanation.surface: A prison guard is the first to knife an inmate from behind.
explanation.walkthrough: LAG reversed is GAL; O stabs into it, giving GAOL, the British spelling of jail.
explanation.definitionFit: Gaol is the traditional British spelling of jail, a place of imprisonment.

clue.text: Small container filled with Askey's earliest material

indicators.note: something filled with an item has that item put inside it

parts.note: S is the abbreviation for small

indicators.note: earliest picks out just the opening letter of the comedian's name

parts.note: Arthur Askey was a British comedian
a tin is a container

explanation.surface: A little box stuffed with the comedian Arthur Askey's first item of fabric.
explanation.walkthrough: S and TIN together form the container; A sits between them.
explanation.definitionFit: Satin is a smooth, glossy fabric, so it is a material in the dressmaking sense.

clue.text: He takes the blame for page's coat getting torn

indicators.note: a coat getting torn is ripped apart, so its letters come out in a new arrangement

parts.note: the letters to rearrange, apostrophe ignored

explanation.surface: A boy is blamed because a page's coat was ripped.
explanation.definitionFit: A scapegoat is a person made to bear the blame for others' wrongdoing.

clue.text: Trouble in a French town

parts.note: un is French for a
Settle is a market town in North Yorkshire

explanation.surface: There is unrest in some French town.
explanation.walkthrough: 'French town' wants to be read together; it is 'a French' and then an English town, Settle in Yorkshire.
explanation.definitionFit: To unsettle someone is to disturb or worry them, which is what to trouble means as a verb.

clue.text: Very much against having son on top, as it were

parts.note: so means very much, as in so tired
pressed against means pressed to
S is the genealogical abbreviation for son
a peak is a top

explanation.surface: Someone strongly opposed to having their boy on top, in a manner of speaking.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Having son on top' puts S above PEAK in this down entry.
explanation.definitionFit: So to speak and as it were are both stock phrases flagging that an expression is figurative.

clue.text: Unsatisfactory to wrap Egyptian goddess in carpet

indicators.note: wrapping something encloses it, so the goddess sits inside the other word

parts.note: a lame excuse is unsatisfactory
Bast, or Bastet, is the Egyptian cat goddess

explanation.surface: It would be poor form to roll an Egyptian goddess up in a rug, as Cleopatra was.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Carpet' looks like a rug; here it is the verb meaning to scold.
explanation.definitionFit: To carpet someone is to reprimand them, and to lambaste is to criticise harshly: both mean a dressing-down.

clue.text: Eats over time to grow

indicators.note: over means finished, so the food word loses its ending where the next piece takes over

parts.note: eats is slang for food, and a burger is food
an eon is a long period of time

explanation.surface: Someone who eats for too long will put on weight.
explanation.walkthrough: The parse is loose: the food word must lose its last two letters before the period of time joins it. 'Eats' is the noun, slang for food.
explanation.definitionFit: To burgeon is to grow or flourish rapidly, as buds do in spring.

clue.text: Essential to stop Ernest becoming a drinker

indicators.note: essential means at the core, so the letters lie inside the run of words

parts.note: the letters run across the two words

explanation.surface: It is vital to stop a man called Ernest from turning into an alcoholic.
explanation.definitionFit: A toper is an old word for a habitual heavy drinker, a boozer.

clue.text: Press it in order to carry on

indicators.note: putting things in order means arranging them afresh, so the letters are sorted anew

parts.note: the letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: An instruction to push a button so that things keep going.
explanation.definitionFit: To persist is to keep going despite difficulty, which is what carry on means.

clue.text: Unusually good fish found in Spain? Just the opposite

indicators.note: something found in something else is inside it
this flips the order, so the country goes inside the fish instead

parts.note: the gar, or garfish, is a long-snouted fish
E is the vehicle code for Spain (España)

explanation.surface: A rare treat: good fish in Spain, or the other way round.
explanation.walkthrough: GEAR as 'great' is 1960s British slang, famously Liverpudlian.
explanation.definitionFit: Gear was Beatles-era slang for excellent or fabulous, so it praises something as exceptionally good.

clue.text: Appears to be speaking to Rex, grabbed by girl from sewer

indicators.note: speaking means we take the sound of the word for appears

parts.note: appears means seems

indicators.note: something grabbed by a person is held within them

parts.note: a girl's name, as in Hardy's Tess
R stands for Rex, king

explanation.surface: Someone seems to be talking to a man called Rex, whom a girl seized from a drain.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sewer' suggests a drain; it is one who sews.
explanation.definitionFit: A seamstress is a woman who sews for a living, so she is a sewer in the needle-and-thread sense.

clue.text: Cut soprano before musical's mentioned

parts.note: S is the abbreviation for soprano

indicators.note: mentioned means said out loud, so we want a word that sounds like the show's name

parts.note: Hair is the 1960s rock musical

explanation.surface: A soprano is dropped before a stage show is talked about.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cut' looks like a verb about the singer; it is the noun meaning a portion.
explanation.definitionFit: A cut is one's portion of the proceeds, so it means a share.

clue.text: Opportunities to sell drink on board

indicators.note: on board a ship means inside the steamship's two letters

parts.note: SS stands for steamship, and anything on board is within it
ale is a drink

explanation.surface: Chances to flog drinks to passengers aboard ship.
explanation.walkthrough: Being on board a ship conventionally means going inside SS.
explanation.definitionFit: Sales are events where goods are offered cheaply, giving shops a chance to shift stock.

clue.text: An animal's place to crash

indicators.note: a crash smashes things up, leaving the letters jumbled

parts.note: the letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: A creature's spot for bedding down for the night.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Place to crash' reads as slang for somewhere to sleep; 'crash' is the anagram signal.
explanation.definitionFit: The polecat is a dark-furred mammal of the weasel family, so it is an animal.

clue.text: City look at containing Villa for the most part

indicators.note: containing means holding the other word inside

parts.note: to look at is to see

indicators.note: most of the word is kept, so its last letter goes

parts.note: taken as written; Aston Villa is a football club

explanation.surface: A city visit to watch the Villa football team.
explanation.definitionFit: Seville is the capital of Andalusia in southern Spain, a major city.

clue.text: Offer of support to keep North Dakota republican

indicators.note: keeping something means holding it within, so the state's letters go inside

parts.note: a golf tee supports the ball
ND is the US postal code for North Dakota
R stands for Republican

explanation.surface: A pledge to back a North Dakota Republican.
explanation.definitionFit: A tender is a formal bid or proposal to supply something, so it is an offer.

clue.text: Swimmers start to seek things to wear on the feet

definitions.meaning: first meaning: flat fish of the ray family

definitions.text: things to wear on the feet
definitions.meaning: second meaning: boots with blades or wheels for gliding

explanation.surface: Swimmers begin hunting for footwear after leaving the pool.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Start to seek' only joins the two meanings; it may hint that the answer starts with the first letter of seek.
explanation.definitionFit: Skate is both a ray-like fish and a bladed or wheeled boot, so the plural covers both senses.
